summary.text: Chemical equilibrium is the state in which reactants and products are both present in concentrations that have no further tendency to change with time.
It results when the forward reaction runs at the same rate as the reverse reaction; those rates are generally not zero, just equal.
Because both reactions keep going with no net change in concentrations, this state is known as dynamic equilibrium.

facts.label: Key condition
facts.value: Forward and reverse reaction rates are equal

facts.label: Response to a disturbance
facts.value: The position moves to partially reverse the change

facts.label: Effect of a catalyst
facts.value: Speeds both directions; the equilibrium constant is unchanged

facts.label: Far to the right
facts.value: Nearly all the reactants are consumed

items.prompt: A sealed mixture shows no change in its concentrations at all. Has the reaction stopped?

options.label: Yes, a lack of change means that nothing is happening
No, the forward and reverse reactions are still going, at equal rates
Yes, because only the forward reaction can ever proceed
No, but only the reverse reaction is still going

items.explain: The forward and backward rates are generally not zero, but they are equal, so there are no net changes in concentration.

items.prompt: Two identical mixtures start reacting, but one has a catalyst added. What differs at the end?

options.label: The catalysed one ends up with a higher equilibrium constant
The catalysed one ends up with a lower equilibrium constant
The constant is the same, but the catalysed one gets there sooner
The uncatalysed one reaches its equilibrium first

items.explain: A catalyst speeds up the forward and reverse reactions in the same way, so it does not change the equilibrium constant but speeds the approach to equilibrium.

items.prompt: At equilibrium, hardly any product has formed from the reactants. Where does the equilibrium position lie?

options.label: Far to the left
Far to the right
Exactly in the middle
Nowhere, because there is no equilibrium

items.explain: A position far to the left means hardly any product is formed from the reactants.

items.prompt: Extra product is poured into a mixture already at equilibrium. How does the system respond?

options.label: The forward reaction increases, pushing further towards products
Neither reaction changes, so the mixture stays put
The equilibrium constant changes to absorb the product
The reverse reaction increases, pushing the equilibrium position backward

items.explain: A disturbed equilibrium moves to partially reverse the change. The equilibrium constant stays the same.

items.prompt: A mixture has settled at equilibrium. How does its reaction quotient compare with the equilibrium constant?

options.label: The quotient is always larger than the constant
The quotient is always smaller than the constant
The two have no fixed relationship to each other
The quotient has the same value as the constant

items.explain: For a system at equilibrium the reaction quotient Q_r equals the equilibrium constant K_eq.

items.prompt: A reaction runs in water. Why is the water's concentration left out of the equilibrium expression?

options.label: Water takes no part in any reaction
Water always has a concentration of zero
As the solvent, its concentration stays high and nearly constant
Water cannot be measured in a mixture

items.explain: H₂O is left out because it is the solvent and its concentration remains high and nearly constant.
